DECISION AND DISMISSAL OF COMPLAINT
On October 17 and October 24, 2024, respectively, Gerald Peters, Jr. (the Complainant)
filed similar individual complaints with the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations
(the Labor Board) alleging that the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 52- Torrington Police
Union (the Union) had committed practices prohibited by the Municipal Employees
Relations Act (MERA or Act). After investigation of the consolidated complaints, the
Agent of the Labor Board recommended dismissal of the complaints. The Agent’s
recommendation was served upon the Complainant by certified mail on December 9,
2024. The Complainant has not filed a written objection to the Agent’s recommendation
for dismissal of the Complaints. Accordingly, pursuant to § 7-471-24 of the Regulations
of Connecticut State Agencies, the complaints are dismissed.

ORDER
Pursuant to the power vested in the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations
by the Municipal Employees Relations Act, it is hereby ORDERED that the complaint
filed herein be and the same hereby is, DISMISSED.

DECISION AND ORDER
On December 13, 2022, the Federation of Technical College Teachers, Local
1942, AFT, AFL-CIO (the Union), filed a complaint with the Connecticut State Board of
Labor Relations (the Labor Board), alleging that the Board of Regents for Higher
Education (the State or BORHE) violated the State Employee Relations Act (the Act) by
failing to comply with an arbitration award.
After the requisite preliminary steps had been taken, the matter came before the
Labor Board for a hearing on January 24, 2024, and February 21, 2024. All parties
appeared, were represented by counsel, and were allowed to present evidence,
examine and cross-examine witnesses, and make argument. The parties filed post-
hearing briefs which were received on May 22, 2024. Based on the entire record before
us, we make the following findings of fact and conclusions of law and issue the
following order.
1

FINDINGS OF FACT
1. BORHE is an employer within the meaning of the Act.
2. The Union is an employee organization within the meaning of the Act and at all
relevant times has represented all faculty members at five State community college
campuses: Naugatuck Valley Community College; Norwalk Community College;
Gateway Community College; Capital Community College; and Three Rivers
Community College.
3. BORHE and the Union were parties to a collective bargaining agreement, with
effective dates of July 1, 2016 through June 30, 2021, which provided, in relevant part:
ARTICLE VIII. PROFESSIONAL WORKING CONDITIONS
***
8.3. ANNUAL WORKLOAD
8.3.1 Teaching Faculty
During each academic year, full-time teaching faculty shall:
8.3.1 Teach twenty-four contract/credit hours and
perform related duties as provided in Section 8.3.5 below.
8.3.1.2 Perform additional responsibilities equivalent
to the preparation and teaching of an additional three contact/credit
course or an average of nine hours per week for each semester
within the appointment year or teach an additional three
contact/credit hours as provided in Section 8.3.6 below. While the
final decision of whether an individual faculty member shall teach
an additional three (3) contact/credit hour course or perform
additional responsibilities rests with management, the managerial
decision shall be based on the merits of each individual faculty
member’s application for additional responsibilities in accordance
with the procedures in Appendix D.
8.3.1.3 The parties agree to the following changes regarding
workload for teaching faculty:
2

a. Full time faculty hired on or after July 1, 2017, shall be
required to teach a course in lieu of Additional
Responsibilities (AR);
***
c. Faculty hired on or after July 1, 2017, shall be released as
appropriate with approval from the colleges so that they may
work on professional obligations toward the goals of
attaining tenure and/or promotion;
d. All faculty employed on or before June 30, 2017 shall elect to
complete AR or teach a 3-credit course for $2,500
compensation . . . Said election shall be made by the faculty
member no later than May 15th of the preceding academic
year. AR approval decisions shall be made no later than June
1st of the preceding academic year. The existing practices and
rules regarding AR proposals/approvals shall remain in
place;
***
8.3.6 Additional Responsibilities/Teaching
8.3.6.1 The additional responsibilities as
specified in Section 8.3.1 may include, but shall not be
limited to the following, and shall be for the purpose of
fulfilling the mission, goals, and priorities of the college and
the System as determined by the employer:
***
(c) development of new instructional techniques, course
offerings or programs, or major revisions of courses or
programs;
***
APPENDIX D
ADDITIONAL RESPONSIBILITIES
In the course of negotiations, the parties have identified shared
concerns regarding the professional responsibilities of teaching beyond
those associated with classroom instruction and related duties. The
3

parties recognize that, as professionals, teaching faculty are expected to
extend their services to meet other institutional needs related to the
mission, goals and priorities of the college and System . . .
To this end, each college shall publish and distribute to all members
of the teaching faculty a comprehensive statement of its institutional
mission, goals and priorities. During the spring semester, each faculty
member will submit a report indicating the specific activities that were
undertaken to meet the obligation of section 8.3.1.2. The report shall
recommend additional responsibilities for the following year...
***
Should it be determined that the statement does not satisfy this
intent or that there are other priorities, the employer will so notify the
faculty member on or before May 1st. The faculty member will be
encouraged to file an amended statement within 15 days of receiving this
notice...
***
APPENDIX X
SIDE LETTER Re: PROTOCOLS FOR DISTANCE LEARNING
***
Course Development
For purposes of this Agreement re: Protocols for Distance Learning,
course development is defined as either (1) creating a new distance
learning course, or (2) converting or adapting an existing on-ground course
to an online format. New courses shall follow existing college course
offerings, development and approval processes.1
1 Appendix X arises from a 2008 interest arbitration award, which stated, in relevant part:
Award the Board’s LBO [last best offer] to maintain current contract language, noting the
Board's express acknowledgment that in the discretion of the Academic Dean, credit
towards additional responsibilities, in increments of one hour for a week to nine hours
per week, may be given for developing a distance learning course.
***
(Ex. R2).
4

***
(Ex. C3, R1).
4. On March 12, 2020, BOR suspended “on-ground” (in-person) classroom
instruction and closed all college campuses due to the onset of the coronavirus
pandemic in Connecticut.
5. In March 2020, faculty at the five community colleges were required to “pivot” to
online instruction, i.e., convert their on-ground courses to remote learning (online)
courses. Remote learning courses resumed on March 23, 2020. (Ex. R10).
6. On June 24, 2020, the Union filed a grievance at Step IV of the grievance
procedure in the collective bargaining agreement, alleging that BORHE violated the
collective bargaining agreement by failing to compensate teaching faculty for
developing and teaching online courses during the spring 2020 and fall 2020
semesters. (Ex. R4)
7. On July 14, 2020, director of labor relations Christopher Henderson denied the
grievance and the Union thereafter filed for grievance arbitration. The parties agreed
upon the following three issues:
1. Did [BORHE] violate Appendix X of its collective bargaining agreement
(CBA) with [the Union] when it did not compensate bargaining unit
members for the development of online courses that went from on-
ground to online in spring 2020?
a. If so, what shall the remedy be pursuant to the CBA?
2. Did [BORHE] violate its Appendix X of its CBA with the Union when it
did not pay the contracted for rate of pay for online courses that went
from on-ground to online in spring 2020?
a. If so, what shall the remedy be pursuant to the CBA?
3. Did [BORHE] violate Appendix X of its CBA with the Union when it did
not apply the contracted for rate of pay for courses developed and
taught online in the fall 2020 semester?
a. If so, what shall the remedy be pursuant to the CBA?
5

***
(Exs. C4, R5).
8. In an award dated June 14, 2021, arbitrator Douglas Cho (Cho or the Arbitrator)
sustained part of the grievance, stating, in relevant part:
SUMMARY OF AWARD
ISSUE #1:
***
Yes, [BORHE] violated Appendix X, since all professors who were required
to pivot from teaching on-ground courses to online classes in Spring 2020
should have received AR credit for their time spent developing online
classes during the Spring 2020, as is allowed under Appendix X, and
consistent with the 2008 Award. The proper remedy is for the affected
faculty members to receive appropriate AR credit in the academic year
2021-2022, or if that is not feasible, then in the following academic year,
2022-2023.
***
(Exs. C4, R5). The Arbitrator answered “no” to the second and third issues.
9. On July 1, 2021, the Union filed a motion to modify or correct the award and
BORHE filed an objection to the Union’s motion on July 12, 2021. (Exs. R6, R7).
10. On July 13, 2021, the Union filed a motion to vacate the award with the Superior
Court for the judicial district of Hartford. (Ex. R9).
11. On August 7, 2021, the Arbitrator denied the Union’s motion to modify or correct
the award. (Ex. R8).
12. In a decision dated March 8, 2022, the Superior Court denied the Union’s
motion to vacate the award. (Ex. R10).
13. Sometime in the fall of 2022, BORHE created a PowerPoint to educate campus
CEOs or campus presidents on the outcome of the arbitration and stating, in relevant
part:
Spring 2020
6

ARBITRATOR’S AWARD
• Faculty Members who were not credited with AR for pivoting to on
line learning during Spring 2020, receive the appropriate AR credit
during the 2022-2023 academic year.
• Recommendation 1 hr/wk/class
*Applicable to those hired prior to July 1 2017 only*
(Exs. C5, R11).
14. In an email to bargaining unit members, the Dean’s Office at Naugatuck Valley
Community College identified the number of AR credits that each would receive in
accordance with the award.
15. At all times relevant hereto, faculty at most campuses utilized an online form to
apply for AR credit. Naugatuck Valley Community College’s online form for the 2022-
2023 academic year gave faculty the option of AR credits under the “AFT arbitration
award for Spring 2020 Pivot...” (Ex. R. 14).
16. The Union steward at Naugatuck Community College, Daniel Picard, polled
each of the faculty and obtained information from the Dean’s Office regarding the AR
credits provided under the arbitration award. Thirty faculty members at Naugatuck
Valley Community College hired before July 1, 2017 received AR credits under the
award. Two faculty hired after June 30, 2017 and seven faculty who converted cases
but in 2020, but who had since retired, did not receive AR credits under the award. (Ex.
C11).
17. At Norwalk Community College, Union steward Peter Daupern polled all
members of the bargaining unit and determined that neither faculty hired prior to July
1, 2017, faculty hired after June 30, 2017, nor faculty who had since retired received
AR credits for converting on-ground courses to remote learning courses in the spring
2020 semester. Norwalk Community College did not notify bargaining unit members of
the availability of such credits and did not use an online AR form during the relevant
time period. (Ex. C7).
18. In fall 2022, the Union also polled faculty at the other campuses and determined
that no colleges other than Naugatuck Valley Community College awarded AR credit to
faculty members under the award. (Exs. C7, C8, C9, C10, C11).
7

19. Sometime prior to November 1, 2022, Union president Dennis Bogusky posed a
series of questions to Connecticut State Community College manager of labor relations
Marilyn Albrecht regarding AR credit. In an email dated November 1, 2022, Albrecht
responded, in relevant part:
1. The amount of AR hours assigned for the course conversion (course
development) were not discussed and agreed to by the faculty member
and the Dean as required by contract and practice.
- The amount of AR in the PowerPoint is a suggestion, which is
why we utilized the “up to language” each individual faculty
member eligible would have discussed the specifics with their
academic deans as outline in the contract since they need to
address the remainder of their AR.
2. Post July 1, 2017 hires are not included.
- Post July 1, 2017, faculty members are not eligible for AR and
the award does not provide an alternative means of
compensation for that pivot outside of what is articulated in the
CBA, Appendix X.
3. Faculty who teach in lieu of AR are not included.
- If a faculty member is opting to teach a fifth class they are
opting to forgo AR.
4. Faculty who taught spring of 2020 and are no longer employed are not
included.
- The award does [sic] provide for any form of compensation for
this work outside what is currently recognized in the agreement
(i.e. AR). AR credit is not available to folks who have retired.
***
(Ex. C6).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. A state employer’s failure or refusal to comply with a valid arbitration award is a
prohibited practice under the Act.
8

2. The Board of Regents for Higher Education violated the Act when it failed to
award AR credit to all actively employed faculty who were required to pivot from
teaching on-ground courses to online classes in Spring 2020.
DISCUSSION
The Union contends that BOR violated § 5-272 of the Act2 by failing to award AR
credits to faculty hired prior to July 1, 2017 at four community college campuses;
refusing to award AR credits to faculty hired after June 30, 2017; and refusing to
compensate faculty who were eligible for the AR credits but who retired or otherwise
separated from their employment prior to implementation of the award.
BORHE responds that the complaint should be dismissed under the doctrine of
laches. Regarding the merits of the Union’s claim, BORHE argues that the award of AR
credits applies only to faculty hired prior to July 1, 2017 and that the Union failed to
prove that any eligible faculty who applied were denied AR credits. According to
BORHE, the collective bargaining agreement does not provide for AR credit to faculty
hired after June 30, 2017, and that, by seeking compensation for retirees, the Union is
pursuing a remedy which was expressly rejected by the arbitrator and the superior
court. Based on the entire record before us, we find that the complaint is timely and
that BORHE violated the Act by failing to award AR credits to all actively employed
faculty who converted on-ground courses to remote learning courses in the spring
2020 semester.
Regarding timeliness of the complaint, “the omission of a statute of limitations
by the Legislature evinces a public policy disfavoring waiver of a complainant’s rights
in a prohibited practice dispute.” State of Connecticut, Department of Public Safety,
Decision No. 2664 p. 5 (1983); see also City of Danbury, Decision No. 5013 (2018); City
of Meriden, Decision No. 4553 (2011). As such, “the doctrine of laches requires a
showing that a party engaged in a delay which was without excuse and that the delay
has prejudiced the other party.” Waterbury Hospital, Decision No. 964 p. 3 (1970);
see also Fay v. Merrill, 338 Conn. 1, 23 (2021) (“The mere lapse of time does not
constitute laches ... unless it results in prejudice to the [opposing party] ... as where,
2 Conn. Gen. Stat. § 5-272 states, in relevant part:
(a) Employers or their representatives or agents are prohibited from: ... (4) refusing to
bargain collectively in good faith with an employee organization which has been
designated in accordance with the provisions of said sections as the exclusive
representative of employees in an appropriate unit; including but not limited to
refusing to discuss grievances with such exclusive representative...
***
9

for example, the [opposing party] is led to change his position with respect to the
matter in question”) (Internal citations and footnote omitted.)
In this case, BORHE contends that the Union’s failure to file the instant
complaint for almost 29 months after it filed its grievance on June 24, 2020, or, in the
alternative, for almost 18 months after the arbitration award was issued, constituted
inexcusable delay and is prejudicial because of the number of faculty who have
retired. Specifically, BORHE argues the Union is seeking financial compensation for
former faculty in lieu of AR credit, and that compelling BORHE to deliver cash
payments to what may be a substantial number of faculty who have separated from
their employment in the intervening period creates an unfair financial burden.
Respondent’s brief, pp. 27-30. We disagree for the following reasons. First, we find that
BORHE’s claim of inexcusable delay fails to account for the fact that, during that time,
the Union pursued contractual and administrative remedies, which, if successful, may
have obviated the need for this complaint. In addition, we find that BORHE’s claim of
prejudice is largely moot given our finding, for the reasons discussed below, that the
award is limited to a prospective grant of AR credit to actively employed faculty.
Accordingly, we decline to dismiss the complaint on laches grounds and turn to the
issue of compliance with the award.
When a party claims that there has been a refusal to comply with an
arbitration award we will interpret the award to ascertain what it requires
and then determine whether the respondent has compiled with those
requirements. State of Connecticut, Office of Policy and Management,
Decision No. 4610 (2012); Town of Middlebury, Decision No. 4603 (2012);
City of Bridgeport, Decision No. 4602 (2012); Town of Enfield, Decision
No. 4461 (2010); City of Willimantic, Decision No. 1795 (1979). We use an
objective standard and we do not consider whether the respondent acted
in good faith or whether its interpretation of the award is a plausible one as
valid defenses. Town of Wallingford, Decision No. 3807 (2001); Town of
Stratford, Decision No. 3277 (1995); City of New Haven, Decision No. 3060
(1992); Town of Newington, Decision No. 2957 (1991); Weston Board of
Education, Decision No. 2678 (1988); Hartford Board of Education,
Decision No. 2683 (1988). Nor is it our function to relitigate or second guess
the merits of grievance decisions. Our role is limited to meeting our
statutory responsibility to insure that the outcome of the grievance
procedure is respected. Connecticut Employees Union Independent (NP-
2 Unit), Decision No. 3446 (1996); City of Waterbury, Decision No. 2195
(1983). As such, our analysis “ ‘only looks to the language of the settlement’
or in this case, the arbitration award.” Town of Enfield, supra at p. 11
(quoting City of Waterbury, Decision No. 3593 (1998). If we find there has
not been compliance, we will find a violation of the Act. Town of
Westbrook, Decision No. 4687 pp. 5-6 (2013); State of Connecticut,
Department of Correction, Decision No. 4475 (2010).
10

***
Town of East Hartford, Decision No. 4907, p. 10 (2016), see also State of
Connecticut, Department of Children and Families, Decision No. 5020 (2018); City
of Waterbury, Decision No. 5009 (2018); Hartford Board of Education, Decision No.
4924 (2016).
Arbitration awards, like judgments, “are to be construed in the same
fashion as other written instruments … [and] should admit of a consistent
construction as a whole … [and] we … ascertain … intent … from the
language used and, if necessary, the surrounding circumstances.”
Wheelabrator Bridgeport, L.P. v. City of Bridgeport, 320 Conn. 332, 355
(2016) (quoting Ottiano v. Shetucket Plumbing Supply Co., 61 Conn. App.
648, 652 (2001)).
State of Connecticut, Department of Children and Families, Decision No. 5062 p. 9
(2019); see also Tannenbaum v. Tannenbaum, 208 Conn. App. 16, 27 (2021).
In this case, we find that the award required BORHE to provide AR credits to
“affected faculty members” and, although the parties dispute the scope of that term,
we ascertain its meaning from the immediately preceding sentence, which states that
“all professors who were required to pivot from teaching on-ground courses to online
classes in Spring 2020 should have received AR credit...” (Exs. C4, R5) (Emphasis
added). Construed as a whole, we find that “affected faculty members” includes both
pre-July 1, 2017 and post-June 30, 2017 faculty who converted courses to remote
learning as part of the Spring 2020 response to the pandemic. However, because the
award also limits the appropriate remedy to AR credits, we find that the award does
not extend to affected faculty who have since separated from their employment and
therefore can no longer benefit from such credits. Id.
BORHE relies on two references to “affected faculty members” elsewhere in the
award to argue that that term should apply only to “faculty members hired before July
1, 2017.” Respondent’s brief, p. 14 (Emphasis added). The first passage upon which
BORHE relies, states, in relevant part:
Another argument offered by [BORHE] is that the affected faculty could
have sought an AR modification in the Spring of 2020 as allowed under the
AR provisions in the Agreement. This is not a convincing, or fundamentally
fair argument. The Union witnesses testified that they had already fulfilled
their allotted AR by mid-March 2020, thus an AR modification was of no
use to them. Moreover, under the Agreement, newer faculty hired
11

beginning in 2017 must teach an additional course rather than get AR, so
those faculty could not benefit from an AR modification...
***
(Exs. C4, R5, p. 14)(Emphasis added). According to BORHE, writing that faculty hired
after June 30, 2017 are excluded from AR credit in the same paragraph as “affected
faculty [who] could have sought an AR modification,” signals an intention to exclude
the former from the award. In the second cited passage, the arbitrator stated, in
relevant part:
all determinations of the appropriate amount of AR credit granted to each
affected faculty member can be awarded consistent with the past
standards for how AR credit has been determined.
***
Id. BORHE argues that this passage “again rules out post-2017 hires receiving
AR, as past practice ... evidences that only pre-2017 hires are eligible for AR.”
Respondent’s brief, p. 14 (Emphasis added).
We find BORHE’s reliance on the first excerpt to be misplaced since, as it
concedes in its brief, the arbitrator is summarizing its position that the Union failed to
use available means to seek redress in 2020. In our view, that passage merely
represents the arbitrator’s acknowledgement that each faculty group has a distinct
reason why it did not seek an AR modification. Moreover, contrary to BORHE’s
assertion, we find that the arbitrator’s blanket rejection of that argument further
evidences that members of either group can fall within the term “affected faculty
members.” 3 Similarly, we read the arbitrator’s reference to “past practice” as nothing
more than an acknowledgement that each dean has a certain amount of discretion to
determine the number of AR credits to be awarded, which is subordinate to the
directive that “all professors” who were required to pivot during the relevant period
are entitled to AR credit. (Ex. C4, R5). As such, the question now becomes whether
BORHE complied with the award.
3 BORHE also relies on an excerpt from the Superior Court decision, denying the motion to
vacate, which stated, in relevant part:
[R]egarding teachers hired after July 2017, the award noted that under the
agreement, newer faculty hired beginning in 2017 must teach an additional
course rather than get AR, so those faculty members also could not benefit from
an AR modification....
***
(Ex. R. 10). However, we think that BORHE’s reliance on this language is misplaced for the same
reasons.
12

BORHE contends that it met its obligation to provide AR credit by educating the
academic deans regarding how to comply with the award, who then delivered a digital
form to certain faculty which provided for AR credit consistent with the award.
Respondent’s brief, p. 18. We are not persuaded. Although BORHE provided guidance
to the administrations of the five colleges, the record reveals that only Naugatuck
Valley Community College acted upon that guidance. The Union produced unrebutted
testimony that Capital Community College, Gateway Community College, Norwalk
Community College and Three Rivers Community College did not award any AR
credits4 and BORHE cannot in our view insulate itself from the failure of those college
administrations to see the matter through to its completion. In sum, we find that the
plain language of the award requires BORHE to afford AR credit to all actively
employed faculty who were required to pivot from teaching on-ground courses to
online classes in Spring 2020 and that, except for faculty hired before July 1, 2017 at
Naugatuck Valley Community College, BORHE did not comply with the award.
Accordingly, we issue the following order.
ORDER
By virtue of and pursuant to the power vested in the Connecticut State Board of
Labor Relations by the State Employee Relations Act, it is hereby
ORDERED that the State of Connecticut Board of Regents for Higher Education
shall:
I. Cease and desist from failing to comply with the arbitration award dated
June 14, 2021.
II. Take the following affirmative actions that we find would effectuate the
purposes of the Act.
A. Provide the Union with a list of all faculty, regardless of date of hire,
currently employed at Naugatuck Valley Community College, Capital
Community College, Gateway Community College, Norwalk
Community College and Three Rivers Community College: who were
required to pivot from teaching on-ground courses to online classes in
Spring 2020; the number of AR credits, if any, awarded to each for
4 CSCU manager of labor relations Marilyn Albrecht testified that a PowerPoint presentation was
distributed to campus CEOs but fell short of saying whether a system of awarding AR to faculty
members was implemented or if any faculty member had received AR credits.
13

time spent developing online classes during the Spring 2020
semester; and the semester in which such credits were awarded.
B. Any faculty members identified in paragraph A, above, who did not
receive AR credits for time spent developing online classes during the
Spring 2020 semester, may elect such credit. BORHE shall award an
appropriate number of said credits to each faculty member in the
Spring 2025 semester.
C. Post immediately and leave posted for a period of sixty (60)
consecutive days from the date of the posting, in a conspicuous place
where the members of the bargaining unit customarily assemble. A
copy of this Decision and Order in its entirety.
D. Notify the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations at its offices at
38 Wolcott Hill Road, Wethersfield, Connecticut, within thirty (30)
days of the receipt of this Decision and Order of the steps taken by the
Board of Regents for Higher Education to comply herewith.

DECISION, ORDER AND PARTIAL
DISMISSAL OF COMPLAINT
On March 23, 2023, the New Haven Fire Union, Local 825, IAFF, AFL-CIO, (the
Union) filed a complaint with the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations (the Labor Board),
amended on August 7, 2023, alleging that the City of New Haven (the City) violated the
Municipal Employee Relations Act (the Act) by transferring the Union president in retaliation for
engaging in protected activity and retracting approval of a proposed settlement agreement in
another prohibited practice complaint.
After the requisite preliminary steps had been taken, the matter came before the Labor
Board for a hearing on November 1 and December 8, 2023, and January 8, February 21, and
March 1, 2024. Both parties appeared, were represented by counsel, and were allowed to present
evidence, examine and cross-examine witnesses, and make argument. The parties filed post-
hearing briefs which were received on April 16, 2024 and reply briefs which were received on
April 30, 2024. Based on the entire record before us, we make the following findings of fact and
conclusions of law, dismiss the complaint in part, and issue the following order.
1

FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The City is an employer within the meaning of the Act.
2. The Union is an employee organization within the meaning of the Act and at all relevant
times has represented all uniformed and investigatory positions in the City’s Department of Fire
Service, except the chief and the department executive officer.
3. The City and the Union were parties to a collective bargaining agreement, with effective
dates of July 1, 2018 through June 30, 2024, which provided, in relevant part:
ARTICLE II
MANAGEMENT RIGHTS
2.1 The employer maintains the exclusive right to direct the work force except
as such right is relinquished, modified, or abridged by or is in conflict with the
terms of this Agreement. This right shall include, but shall not be limited to, the
right to:
***
(b) hire, promote, transfer and assign;
***
ARTICLE VI – GRIEVANCE PROCEDURE
***
Step 1
The Union shall submit such grievance in writing to the Chief of the Fire
Department... [The Chief] or his designated representative shall arrange to and shall
meet with the grievant and representatives of the Union for the purpose of adjusting
or resolving such grievance.
***
ARTICLE VII – UNION ACTIVITIES
***
2

7.7 … [T]he City agrees to release the Union President to attend to Union
Business during his day tours[1] without a loss of pay.
***
ARTICLE XXX – WAGES
***
30.8 Members of the Department who function in the capacity of ... Driver ...
during a shift shall receive an additional one dollar and fifty cents ($1.50) per hour
for those hours actually worked in these capacities. The stipend will not be paid
during any leave time (personal, sick, vacation, etc.)
***
(Ex. R1) (Footnote added).
4. Since approximately 1999, Patrick Cannon has been a firefighter in the City Fire
Department and at all relevant times has been the Union president.
5. Effective October 21, 2000, then-chief Dennis Daniels transferred Cannon to Truck 1,
Division 1. (Ex. R2).
6. Effective January 7, 2009, then-chief Michael E. Grant transferred Cannon from Truck 1,
Division 1 to the driver of Truck 1, Division 3. As such, Cannon earned an additional $1.50 per
hour while actively driving. (Ex. R3).
7. In a memorandum to then-chief of staff Sean Matteson dated December 17, 2010, then-
City corporation counsel Victor Bolden opined, in relevant part:
Pursuant to Section 7-474(a) of the General Statutes, the Mayor of New Haven, or
his or her “designated representative” represents the City in all collective
bargaining matters, and enjoys the exclusive authority to negotiate agreements
between the City and recognized employee organizations. In New Haven, the
Mayor's designated representative is the Director of Labor Relations…
***
(Ex. R9).
1 At all times relevant hereto, City firefighters have worked a schedule of three consecutive 10-hour “day” tours,
followed by three consecutive days off, and three consecutive 14-hour “night” tours. Section 7.7 of the collective
bargaining agreement provides Union presidents with full-time release from their day tour assignments.
3

8. In approximately 2016, the City hired John Alston as the fire chief.
9. On June 15, 2021, Alston issued General Order #21-03 transferring 15 members of the
City Fire Department. (Ex. R6).
10. On January 14, 2022, Alson issued General Order #22-01 transferring 52 members of the
City Fire Department, including firefighter Scotte Pullen. Ten days later, on January 24th, the
Union filed a prohibited practice complaint with the Labor Board (MPP-34,580), alleging that
the City involuntarily transferred Pullen in retaliation for engaging in protected, concerted
activity. (Exs. C15, R7).
11. In February 2022, Wendella A. Battey succeeded Cathleen Simpson as the City’s director
of labor relations. Prior to Simpson, Thomas McCarthy was the City’s director of labor relations.
12. In March 2022, Battey instructed City department heads and other members of
management that only the director of labor relations or her designee had the authority to bind the
City to an agreement with a union.2
13. In 2022, because Cannon was on Union leave, he performed little or no driving duties. As
such, Cannon did not receive the driver’s stipend. In Cannon’s absence, firefighter Stephen
Maldonado drove Truck 1.
14. In July 2022, Pullen retired. The Union did not withdraw MPP-34,580. (Ex. C8).
15. On or about February 1, 2023, in the hallway of the Fire Department, assistant chief of
administration Justin McCarthy asked Cannon and Union vice president Daniel DelPrete about
the status of MPP-34,580. During that conversation, McCarthy commented on the Union’s
decision to continue to pursue Pullen’s complaint and said something to the effect that the
transfer list is coming out and that “nobody is safe.”
16. On February 4 or 5, 2023, Alston finalized a new transfer list. Alston was not aware of
the conversation between McCarthy, Cannon, and DelPrete.
17. On February 6, 2023, the Union’s counsel in the Pullen matter had a subpoena served
which commanded City assistant chief Terrance Roundtree to testify at a Labor Board hearing on
MPP-34,580 scheduled for February 8, 2023. (Ex. C5).
18. On February 7, 2023, Alston issued a General Order transferring 62 members of the City
Fire Department, including Cannon and Maldonado. In a letter of even date, Alston notified
Cannon that he was being transferred from Truck 1, Division 3 to Engine 16, Division 4,
2 Fire chief Alston testified that each labor relations director set their own rules regarding who could enter into such
settlements. Alston testified that he signed 1-2 settlement agreements under former labor relations director Thomas
McCarthy, that he did not recall signing any under Simpson, and that did not sign agreements any under Battey.
4

effective February 16, 2023. Alston transferred Maldonado into Cannon’s assignment as the
driver of Truck 1, Division 3.3 (Exs. R4, R12).
19. On February 13, 2023, the City hired Curtis Stubbs as a staff attorney in the Office of
Labor Relations. Stubbs worked under Battey’s direct supervision.
20. On or about April 4, 2023, after Cannon objected to being transferred, Alston reassigned
Cannon as the driver of Truck 1, Division 3. (Ex. R5).
21. On May 31, 2023, the parties attended a preliminary conference in this case (MPP-
34,976) with an assistant labor board agent. The Union was represented by attorney Marshal
Segar and Cannon and DelPrete attended in their capacity as Union officers. Stubbs represented
the City and Alston attended in his capacity as fire chief. The meeting took place in City Hall.
Battey did not attend the meeting, but was in her office on the next floor.
22. The parties discussed settlement and the Union’s counsel produced a handwritten
proposed settlement of MPP-34,976 and MPP-34,580, which included the following provisions:
d) From July 1, 2023 - June 30, 2024 the Union Vice President shall have
Union release time consistent with such leave afforded to the Union President in
accordance with the CBA.
e) From July 1, 2023 - June 30, 2024 the Union president shall enjoy “full
time” release subject to notice to the Chief of the Department.
3 In response to a question about his rationale for transferring Cannon, Alston testified, in relevant part:
A Well, at that time there was a young man, Steve Maldonado, who was filling in, in that
driver position where Mr. Cannon was the assigned driver. He had proven himself over and over
again and had requested to be transferred and get the driving job. We did not give it to him initially
because, as they stated before, it's a coveted position. But people look - it doesn't mean that you
cannot be transferred; it just means that you own that spot. And he had been performing so well and
Mr. Cannon had not been there, it was my decision to place him in there to reward him, to
acknowledge him for the great job that he was doing.
Q Okay. “He” being Mr. Maldonado?
A Correct.
Q Okay. Now, when you said Mr. Cannon wasn't there, what do you mean by that?
A Mr. Cannon was off a lot due to union business, which is allowed in the collective
bargaining agreement. There is no loss of money; you only get paid the driver stipend when you're
in the seat. So, there was really no financial impact to Mr. Cannon.
***
J. Alston testimony, Tr. 12/08/24, pp. 91-92.
5

***
(Ex. C10).
23. Cannon reviewed the settlement agreement and Alston indicated that he “didn’t see a
problem with it.” Stubbs took the proposed agreement to Battey. However, Battey rejected it.
Neither Stubbs nor Alston represented that they did or did not have authority to bind the City to
the proposed settlement.
24. On or about June 3, 2023, Segar emailed another proposed settlement to Stubbs, which,
among other things, provided the Union vice president with similar rights to Union business
leave as the president under certain circumstances. The City did not agree to the proposal. (Ex.
R8).
25. In August 2023, the parties attended another preliminary conference on this case.
However, no settlement was reached.
26. In or about October 2023, Battey learned that the police chief had executed an agreement
with the police union. Sometime thereafter, in October, 2023, Battey issued a memorandum
reiterating that the director of labor relations has exclusive authority to bind the City.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. Employer discrimination and retaliation against employees for engaging in protected,
concerted activity is a violation of the Act.
2. The City violated the Act by transferring the Union president in retaliation for taking
Union business leave.
3. The Union and the City did not agree to a settlement on May 31, 2023.
DISCUSSION
The Union contends that the City transferred Cannon in retaliation for conducting Union
business4 and retracted its approval of a settlement agreement in violation of Sections 7-
470(a)(1)(2)(3) and (4) of the Act.5 Specifically, the Union argues that Alston admitted that he
4 The Union appears to have abandoned its original argument that the City retaliated against Cannon because the
Union subpoenaed Roundtree. However, even if we were to consider that claim, we find that Alston’s testimony that
he finalized the transfer list 24-48 hours before the Roundtree subpoena was served makes it unlikely that the Union
could establish a prima facie case.
5 Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-470 provides, in relevant part:
(a) Municipal employers or their representatives or agents are prohibited from: (1) Interfering,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7-468; (2)
dominating or interfering with the formation, existence or administration of any employee
organization; (3) discharging or otherwise discriminating against an employee because he has signed
6

transferred Cannon because of Cannon’s use of Union business leave. Regarding the alleged
settlement agreement, the Union argues that the City was bound by its terms under the doctrine
of apparent authority.
The City responds that the Union failed to prove anti-union animus. The City further
argues that, even if the Union proved its prima facie case, the City would have nevertheless
transferred Cannon for a legitimate operational reason; specifically, to season less experienced
firefighters. Lastly, the City contends that the Union failed to establish that Stubbs had apparent
authority to bind the City to the terms of a settlement agreement. Based on the entire record
before us, we find that the City violated the Act by transferring Cannon from the driver’s
position. However, we also find that neither Stubbs nor Alston had apparent authority to bind the
City to the terms of the proposed settlement agreement and dismiss that portion of the complaint.
Our standard for assessing claims of wrongful discrimination or retaliation in response to
protected activity is well established:
A complainant alleging that employees were discriminated against in their
employment because of [protected, concerted] activity has the initial burden of
showing that the discriminatory action was taken because of these protected
activities, or at least that the protected activities were a substantial factor in bringing
about these adverse actions. Town of Greenwich, Decision No. 2257 (1983), aff’d
O’Brien v. State Board of Labor Relations, 8 Conn. App. 57 (1986); Connecticut
Yankee Catering Co., Inc. Decision No. 1601 (1977). We determine whether the
complainant has met this burden to establish a prima facie case of discrimination
using an analytical framework such as is found in Wright Line, 251 NLRB 1083,
enfd 622 F.2d 899 (1st Cir. 1981), cert denied 455 U.S. 989 (1982). “A prima facie
case includes proof that: (1) the employee engaged in protected, concerted
activities; (2) the employer had knowledge of those activities; and (3) the employer
harbored anti-union animus.” New Britain Board of Education, Decision No. 4290
p. 4 (2008). Once a prima facie case is established, we then address whether the
employer has established an affirmative defense which may include proof that the
employer would have pursued its course of conduct regardless of any anti-union
motivation. City of Hartford, Decision No. 3785 (2000); New Fairfield Board of
Education, Decision No. 3327 (1995).
or filed any affidavit, petition or complaint or given any information or testimony under sections 7-
467 to 7-477, inclusive; (4) refusing to bargain collectively in good faith with an employee
organization which has been designated in accordance with the provisions of said sections as the
exclusive representative of employees in an appropriate unit;
***
Section 7-470(a)(2) is concerned with circumstances where an employer inserts itself into the structure or operation
of what purports to be a labor organization, thereby creating a so-called “company union.” See Town of Windham,
Decision No. 4859 (2016); Town of Cheshire, Decision No. 4809 (2015); New Fairfield Board of Education,
Decision No. 3327 (1995). Since the record is devoid of evidence or argument material to such issue we dismiss the
Union’s claim under that section.
7

***
City of Shelton, Decision No. 5212 pp. 8-9 (2021) and cases cited therein.
In this case, Alston was aware of Cannon’s Union business leave, and since using such
leave to conduct Union business is protected, concerted activity, we find that the Union has
satisfied the first two elements of a prima facie case of retaliation. Regarding animus, given
Alston’s testimony that he transferred Cannon because Cannon was “off a lot due to union
business,”6 we find that this case is an exception to the general rule that “direct evidence of
improper motive … is rarely available.” Connecticut Yankee Catering Co., Decision No. 1601 p.
5 (1977). Based on that evidence, we find that the Union has proved its prima facie case and
turn to the City’s defenses.
The City contends that it would have transferred Cannon regardless of any improper
motivation; specifically, to professionally develop less experienced firefighters. We are not
persuaded. Assuming that Alston had a legitimate operational reason to transfer Maldonado to a
driver’s position, his testimony establishes that he transferred Maldonado into Cannon’s position
because Cannon was away performing Union business.7 Moreover, Alston’s testimony that
Maldonado had previously been denied the position raises an inference that Cannon’s continuing
Union leave was the dispositive factor in this instance. Even couched in terms of “low impact”,8
Alston’s conclusions are impermissibly linked to the protected activity in this case.
Regarding whether Stubbs had the authority to bind the City:
An agent’s authority may be actual or apparent.... Actual authority exists when [an
agent's] action [is] expressly authorized ... or ... although not authorized, [is]
subsequently ratified by the [principal].” (Citations omitted; internal quotation
marks omitted.) Maharishi School of Vedic Sciences, Inc. (Connecticut) v.
Connecticut Constitution Associates Ltd. Partnership, 260 Conn. 598, 606–607
(2002). In contrast, “[a]pparent authority is that semblance of authority which a
principal, through his own acts or inadvertences, causes or allows third persons to
believe his agent possesses.... Consequently, apparent authority is to be determined,
not by the agent's own acts, but by the acts of the agent’s principal … The issue of
apparent authority is one of fact to be determined based on two criteria . . . First, it
must appear from the principal’s conduct that the principal held the agent out as
possessing sufficient authority to embrace the act in question, or knowingly
permitted [the agent] to act as having such authority.... Second, the party dealing
with the agent must have, acting in good faith, reasonably believed, under all the
6 See Footnote 3, supra.
7 Footnote 3, supra. See also Tr. 12/08/23, p. 113 (“Transferring [Cannon] was low impact. It didn't impact his
finances; It didn't impact him coming to work. He had a pattern of not coming to work…”).
8 We also believe that Alston underestimated the impact of depriving Cannon of a “coveted” position. Footnote 3,
supra.
8

circumstances, that the agent had the necessary authority to bind the principal to
the agent’s action . . .
***
Waterbury Board of Education, Decision No. 5182 p.10 (2021).
The Union contends that, in light of the history of department heads and other designated
City representatives executing settlement agreements, the City cloaked Stubbs in apparent
authority by permitting him to negotiate settlement terms without disclosing that he lacked
authority to execute an agreement. In addition, the Union argues that Alston expressed his
support for the agreed upon terms, which further contributed to a good faith reasonable belief
that Stubbs could settle the complaint. We are not persuaded.
The Union largely relies on Alston’s testimony to establish the settlement authority of
department heads and other City representatives prior to Battey’s tenure. However, in this
instance, the Union’s reliance is misplaced. Alston testified that he signed a maximum of two
settlement agreements during McCarthy’s tenure as labor relations director. However, Alston also
testified that each labor relations director sets their own rules regarding settlement authority and
that he did not sign any agreements under Simpson or Battey.9 The only evidence of another
department head settling a labor matter is Battey’s testimony concerning the chief of police.
However, the Union has failed to establish that that settlement occurred prior to the May 31,
2023 preliminary conference, and, if so, that the Union was aware of it. As such, we find that that
evidence is not relevant. Moreover, Battey’s negative reaction indicates that the police chief’s
action was an unwelcome departure from the general rule. In addition, we credit Battey’s
testimony that, since her appointment, she had in fact been exercising exclusive authority to enter
into settlements with the unions and that Stubbs was new to the job and had not yet exercised
independent authority in labor relations matters. Under these circumstances, we find that the
City’s decision to send Stubbs to the informal conference, and Stubbs participation in negotiating
the terms of a potential settlement does not give rise to a reasonable belief the he could or did
bind the City. As such, we find that the Union has failed to establish apparent authority and
dismiss this portion of the complaint.10
Regarding the remedy for retaliation, although Alston’s decision to rescind Cannon’s
transfer did not preclude a finding of liability, it is relevant to remedy. Since the record reveals
that the harm caused by Cannon’s transfer was largely cured by subsequently returning him to his
original position, we find that a cease and desist order will adequately effectuate the policies of
the Act and issue the following order.
ORDER
9 We discount Alston’s testimony that he settled grievances. To the extent that Article VI of the contract grants
settlement authority to the fire chief it is expressly limited to step one of the grievance procedure. As such, it cannot
in our view support a reasonable belief that such authority applied here.
10 The City contends that the apparent authority doctrine does not apply to public employers. We do not address this
argument since the record before us does not support a finding that Stubbs had apparent authority.
9

By virtue of and pursuant to the power vested in the Connecticut State Board of Labor
Relations by the Municipal Employee Relations Act, it is hereby
ORDERED that the City of New Haven:
I. Cease and desist from discriminating against employees for engaging in protected,
concerted activity.
II. Take the following affirmative steps which the Board finds will effectuate the
purposes of the Act:
A. Post and leave posted for a period of sixty (60) consecutive days from the date of
such posting, in a conspicuous place where the employees customarily assemble,
a copy of this Decision, Order and Partial Dismissal of Complaint in its entirety;
and
B. Notify the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations at its offices in the Labor
Department, 38 Wolcott Hill Road, Wethersfield, Connecticut, within thirty (30)
days of the receipt of this Decision, Order and Partial Dismissal of Complaint of
the steps taken by the City of New Haven to comply therewith.

STATE OF CONNECTICUT
LABOR DEPARTMENT
CONNECTICUT STATE BOARD OF LABOR RELATIONS
IN THE MATTER OF
HARTFORD BOARD OF EDUCATION
DECISION NO. 5334
-and-
OCTOBER 03, 2024
HARTFORD FEDERATION
OF TEACHERS, LOCAL 1018,
AFT CT, AFL-CIO
Case No. TPP-34,959
A P P E A R A N C E S:
Attorney Lori A. Mizerak
for the School Board
Attorney Eric W. Chester
for the Union
DECISION, ORDER AND PARTIAL DISMISSAL OF COMPLAINT
On March 10, 2023, the Hartford Federation of Teachers, Local 1018, AFT CT,
AFL-CIO (the Union) filed a complaint with the Connecticut State Board of Labor
Relations (the Labor Board), amended on July 17, 2023, alleging that the Hartford Board
of Education (the School Board) violated the School Board-Teacher Negotiation Act
(TNA or the Act) by coercing and/or retaliating against members for exercising protected
rights.
After the requisite preliminary steps had been taken, the matter came before the
Labor Board for a hearing on October 18, 2023. Both parties appeared, were represented
by counsel, and were given full opportunity to present evidence, examine and cross-
examine witnesses, and make arguments. Both parties submitted post-hearing briefs on
January 12, 2024. Based on the entire record before us, we make the following findings
of fact and conclusions of law, dismiss the complaint in part, and issue the following
order.

FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The School Board is a local board of education under the Act.
2. The Union is an organization of certified professional employees under the Act
and at all relevant times has been the exclusive bargaining representative for a unit of
public school teachers employed by the School Board, including special education
teachers.
3. At all times relevant hereto, the School Board and the Union were parties to a
collective bargaining agreement, effective July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025, which
states, in relevant part:
ARTICLE XIII – PROFESSIONAL STATUS
***
C. Union-Superintendent Meeting
The Superintendent of Schools and representatives of the Union shall meet
at the request of either party on a monthly basis to discuss matters of
educational policy and professional concern…
1. The Union Committee for this purpose shall consist of three to
five members. [1]
2. The Superintendent may meet in person or through his/her
designated representative and may include at the meeting such
members of his/her administrative staff as he/she may desire.
3. The Union and the Superintendent will submit, at least one
week in advance of such meeting, items which they wish to be
placed on the agenda for discussion.
***
(Ex. C4) (Footnote added).
4. At all times relevant hereto, the School Board used the Zoom video conferencing
platform to conduct Union-Superintendent Meetings and, as the host, controlled who is
admitted into the meeting from the virtual waiting room.
1 Prior to the meeting on February 23, 2023, the Union had filed a grievance alleging that the School Board
violated the collective bargaining agreement by refusing to allow an AFT filed representative Union to
attend. That grievance had been submitted to arbitration and an award sustaining the grievance was issued
on May 2, 2023. (Ex. C6).
2

5. On February 1, 2023, Union president Carol Gale attended a Union meeting with
special education teachers to discuss working conditions, including high turnover and
recruitment and retention strategies. Special education team leader Raquel Barrows was
selected to present members’ concerns at the next Union-Superintendent Meeting, which
was scheduled for Monday, February 13, 2023. Barrows was also the Union building
representative at Hartford Public High School (HPHS). (Ex. C6).
6. In an email to the Superintendent’s executive secretary dated February 10, 2023,
at 10:05 a.m., Gale provided the Union’s meeting agenda, which included “SPED[2]
concerns - presented by Raquel Barrows… ” as the second of five items. Acting deputy
superintendent of academics Madeline Negron requested that item two be moved to a
separate meeting. However, the Union refused. Negron then asked to move the item to
the top of the agenda and the Union agreed. (Ex. C7).
7. In an email to assistant superintendent for special education Jennifer Hoffman
dated February 11, 2023, at 10:53 a.m., Negron stated, in relevant part, “I will need you
at Monday’s [Union-Superintendent] meeting which starts at 11 a.m. We will hear
concerns related to SPED that [Gale] added to the agenda…” (Ex. R3).
8. On February 13, 2023, Negron and Hoffman attended the Union-Superintendent
Meeting for the School Board. The Superintendent was not online.3 Gale and Union vice
presidents Corey Moses and Stuart Beckford were admitted into the meeting. Barrows
remained in the virtual waiting room. Negron asked whether the Union would present
their special education concerns and Gale refused because the superintendent was not
present. The parties agreed to move to other agenda items and Barrows left or was
removed from the virtual waiting room by approximately 11:15 a.m. The superintendent
subsequently signed into the meeting. However, the special education items were not
discussed.
9. Shortly after the meeting ended, on February 13, 2023, Hoffman emailed Barrows
stating that she would be at HPHS and asking to connect. Barrows agreed to meet to
discuss compliance issues, but declined to meet without the Union leadership if Hoffman
wished to discuss special education teachers’ concerns. Hoffman did not meet with
Barrows. (Ex. C9).
10. On February 21, 2023, during the public comment portion of a regular meeting of
the Hartford Board of Education, Gale read her notes from the February 1, 2023 meeting
of special education teachers into the record. (Ex. R1).
2 “SPED” stands for Special Education.
3 Negron did not state whether or not she was the superintendent’s “designee” and Gale was not given
advance notice that the superintendent would not be at the meeting.
3

11. At all times relevant hereto, Mary Cristofaro has been the director of special
education responsible for seven Hartford schools, including HPHS. As such, Cristofaro
routinely attended monthly SPED compliance meetings with special education teachers in
her assigned schools. Cristofaro reported to Hoffman.
12. At all times relevant hereto, SPED compliance meetings in the Hartford school
district typically consisted of uploading a document to an electronic SMART board
listing relevant issues, such as enrollment, PPT's,4 caseloads, student contact hours,
staffing concerns, and legislation. Notes are typically taken directly on the Smartboard
document and staffing is a common issue. The final portion of the meeting is devoted to
discussing other SPED issues and fielding questions.
13. Hoffman formally observes the individuals whom she supervises four times per
year to evaluate their performance. Sometime prior to March 2, 2023, Hoffman allowed
her supervisees to select the work environment in which they would be observed.
Cristofaro chose to be observed at a SPED compliance meeting.
14. On March 2, 2023, Hoffman attended a SPED compliance meeting with
Cristofaro at HPHS. Barrows was among the teachers present at the meeting. Later that
day, in an email to Cristofaro, with copies to the Union and others, Barrows stated, in
relevant part:
In a compliance meeting this morning ... you brought up a Union matter
presented by Carol Gale at the [School Board] Meeting on Tuesday March
1, 2023. You then specifically asked, “Ms. Barrows are you writing this
down?” This is a cause for concern as I felt as if I was being singled out...
Of further concern are other statements made in this conversation such as:
• Reminding the 8 teachers that were there that our job is a school
board job and is programmatic and we can be moved at any time...
• “Teachers leave all the time and there is nothing that can be done
about it.”
• You repeatedly said when you are asking for things to be done,
“we should be cautious because we may not like some of the
actions that are taken and that we need to think about things before
we speak.”
• “We should fix things in-house before we take it to the Union.”
• We (HPHS)“are the only school with 2 ninth grade teachers and
we should consider ourselves lucky.”
You stated that you “Do not care if whatever you say goes back to the union,”
therefore I have included them in this email. Moving forward I ask that you
4 “PPT” is an acronym for Planning and Placement Team.
4

refrain from singling me out or in any way discriminating against me for my
participation or non-participation in protected activities.
***
(Ex. C8). Cristofaro did not reply to Barrows’ email.
15. On March 2, 2023, Gale emailed Cristofaro regarding Barrows’ email, stating, in
relevant part, that she was also concerned about the way in which members were being
treated, warning Cristofaro against interfering with members’ rights, and reminding her
that the Union has a role in all labor matters. Cristofaro did not reply to the email. (Exs.
R2, R4).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. It is a prohibited practice for a municipal employer to interfere, restrain, or coerce
employees in the exercise of rights guaranteed in § 10-153a of the Act.
2. The School Board did not interfere with bargaining unit members’ rights to present
workplace issues to management through a chosen representative at the February 13,
2023 meeting.
3. The School Board, through its director of special education, made statements at the
March 2, 2023 compliance meeting which would reasonably tend to interfere with the
exercise of rights guaranteed in § 10-153a of the Act.
4. It is a prohibited practice and a violation of the Act for an employer to negotiate a
bargaining unit member’s terms or conditions of employment directly with the member.
5. The School Board did not engage in direct dealing.
DISCUSSION
The Union contends that the School Board violated § 10-153e(b)(1)5 of the Act
5 Conn. Gen. Stat. § 10-153e states, in relevant part:
(b) The local or regional board of education or its representatives or agents are prohibited
from: (1) Interfering, restraining or coercing certified professional employees in the
exercise of the rights guaranteed in sections 10-153a to 10-153n …
***
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 10-153a states, in relevant part:
(a) Members of the teaching profession shall have and shall be protected in the exercise
of the right to form, join or assist, or refuse to form, join or assist, any organization for
professional or economic improvement and to negotiate in good faith through
5

by interfering with its members’ ability to present workplace concerns to management
through an appointed representative. Specifically, the Union argues that Negron
repeatedly attempted to remove SPED concerns from the agenda of the Union-
Superintendent meeting and refused to admit Barrows. In addition, the Union argues that
Hoffman’s email shortly after the meeting and Cristofaro’s statements at the compliance
meeting were attempts to intimidate and retaliate against Barrows. Lastly, the Union
argues that Hoffman engaged in direct dealing by trying to arrange a face-to-face meeting
with Barrows.
The School Board responds that, at the February 13, 2023 meeting, it gave the
Union an opportunity to present its SPED concerns to Negron, who was the
superintendent’s “designee” within the meaning of Article XIII of the collective
bargaining agreement. However, the School Board argues, the Union refused that
opportunity. Moreover, the School Board argues that the Union cannot meet its burden of
proving that Negron, Hoffman or Cristofaro acted with anti-union animus. Based on the
entire record before us, we find that some of Cristofaro’s statements at the compliance
meeting constituted interference, restraint and coercion, issue the following order, and
dismiss the remainder of the complaint.
The Union-Superintendent Meeting
Section 10-153a of the Act protects teachers in their right to engage in Union and
protected concerted activities, and Section 10-153e of the Act makes it a prohibited
practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or coerce such teachers in the exercise
of those rights. However, we find that no illegal coercion, interference, or restraint with
statutory rights occurred at or immediately after the Union-Superintendent Meeting.
Negron’s requests to move the SPED discussion to another meeting was only that, a
request, as demonstrated by her email invitation to Hoffman two days earlier and by
Hoffman’s presence at the meeting. Regarding the meeting itself, the School Board had a
collectively bargained right to meet with the Union through the superintendent or her
designee and the record reveals that Gale’s refusal to present SPED issues to anyone but
the superintendent was a substantial factor in the breakdown of the meeting, including
Barrows remaining in the virtual waiting room.
The Union disputes that Negron was the superintendent’s designee, largely
because she did not identify herself as such.6 However, the record reveals that Negron
representatives of their own choosing with respect to salaries, hours and other conditions
of employment free from interference, restraint, coercion or discriminatory practices by
any employing board of education or administrative agents or representatives thereof in
derogation of the rights guaranteed by this section ...
***
6 Gale testified that the superintendent typically notified Gale that she would not be attending a meeting.
However, we find that the record in that regard is not sufficiently developed to support the existence of
binding practice or provide a basis for finding that Negron was not the superintendent’s designee.
6

announced that the superintendent was unavailable and was never asked whether she was
the superintendent’s designee. In this context, we believe that the presence of the acting
deputy superintendent of academics and assistant superintendent for special education at
a meeting, in which there were SPED issues on the agenda, raised a reasonable inference
that they had been designated to act for the superintendent. In addition, we believe that
the Union could rely on the fact that speaking to Negron and Hoffman in this instance
would have the same weight and effect as speaking directly to the superintendent.
However, the Union declined. Accordingly, we find that the School Board did not deny
the Union an opportunity to present its SPED concerns.
Hoffman and Cristofaro
The Union further argues that Hoffman’s request to meet directly with Barrows,
and Cristofaro’s statements at the compliance meeting, constituted interference and/or
retaliation. At the outset, we note that both parties apply the analytical framework derived
from Wright Line, 251 NLRB 1083, enf’d, 622 F.2d 899 (1st Cir. 1981), cert. denied,
455 U. S. 989 (1982).7 However, we decline to utilize that standard here given the nature
of the alleged violations.
The “Wright Line [analysis] generally applies … where the
employer is alleged to have taken adverse employment action
against an employee and the factual inquiry focuses on the
employer's intent in doing so” with the “attendant requirement that
a complainant demonstrate the existence of antiunion motive…”
AFSCME, AFL-CIO, Council 4, Local 2405 v. City of Norwalk,
156 Conn. App. 79, 91, 93 (2015); see also City of New Haven,
Decision No. 4720 p. 4 (2014)...
***
State of Connecticut Department of Correction, Decision No. 4914 pp. 6-7 (2016).
There is no evidence of any adverse employment action here and we construe the
Union’s claim to be that Hoffman’s and Cristofaro’s statements were inherently coercive.
As such, the Union need not establish anti-union animus. Rather,
The standard … entails determining whether “under all the existing
circumstances, the [employer's] conduct has a reasonable tendency to
coerce or intimidate employees, regardless of whether they are actually
coerced” … By its very language, this test is inconsistent with Wright
7 Under the Wright Line burden-shifting analysis, the complainant has the burden to establish a prima facie
case of discrimination. “A prima facie case includes proof that: (1) the employee engaged in protected,
concerted activities; (2) the employer had knowledge of those activities; and (3) the employer harbored
anti-union animus. … Once a prima facie case is established, we then address whether the employer has
established an affirmative defense which may include proof that the employer would have pursued its
course of conduct regardless of any anti-union motivation..” City of New Haven, Decision No. 5319 p. 5
(2024) and cases cited therein
7

Line because it considers an employer's motive, i.e., antiunion animus, to
be irrelevant … Conduct that tends to coerce or intimidate employees
includes, inter alia, “threats of discharge in retaliation for union activity ...
grants or promises to grant benefits to discourage employee support for a
union ... the cultivated impression that employees' union activities are
under surveillance ... coercive interrogations of employees concerning
their union activity ... and, in certain circumstances, threats of plant
closure.” (Citations omitted; internal quotation marks omitted) …
AFSCME, AFL-CIO, Council 4, Local 2405 v. City of Norwalk, supra at 91; see also
State of Connecticut Department of Correction, supra.
Whether the statements at issue here had a reasonable tendency to coerce or
intimidate turns, in part, on a credibility determination which we resolve in favor of
Hoffman and Cristofaro. Hoffman testified that her duties include fielding SPED
concerns, and while Barrows testified that it would be out of the ordinary for the assistant
superintendent for special education to reach out to special education teachers, she also
testified that she has spoken directly to Hoffman in the past. Moreover, in this instance,
Barrows was the Union’s designated spokesperson and we do not believe that Hoffman’s
request to communicate with that spokesperson shortly after a failed attempt to conduct a
virtual meeting, without more, would reasonably tend to coerce or intimidate.
We also credit Cristofaro’s testimony regarding the substance of her statements at
the compliance meeting and the context in which she made them. Specifically, Cristofaro
testified that she did not bring up Union issues but merely responded to questions
regarding some of the issues raised by Gale during the Board of Education meeting, such
as teacher retention. Cristofaro also credibly testified that teachers typically take notes
electronically, which are reflected on the Smartboard document. According to Cristofaro,
Barrows sat down next to her and began writing on a pad of paper, which prompted
Cristofaro to ask whether Barrows was taking notes. Cristofaro did not direct Barrows to
stop. Lastly, Cristofaro denied saying anything about the Union when she referred to
teachers fixing problems “in-house.”
In our view, the majority of Cristofaro’s statements, viewed in that context, did
not violate the Act. Specifically, we think that Cristofaro’s response that teachers leave
for a variety of reasons would likely be viewed as a simple statement of fact or opinion
and that her inquiry into Barrow’s notetaking would not reasonably tend to intimidate
absent a directive to stop. Moreover, we find that Cristofaro’s statements regarding fixing
problems “in house” merely promoted the type of school-specific problem solving
embodied in the compliance meetings. Nor did it disparage the Union. Under these
circumstances, we do not think that Cristofaro’s statement can be reasonably construed as
having a tendency to restrain a reasonable employee from exercising his or her right to
seek the assistance of the bargaining agent.
Cristofaro’s statement that HPHS is fortunate to have two 9th grade special
education teachers is more problematic. Barrows is a 9th grade SPED teacher, and, in our
8

view, Cristofaro’s observation, together with her statements concerning teacher transfers,
less than one month after an abortive union-management meeting on SPED issues, could
be reasonably construed as an implied threat which would tend to make an employee
think twice about accepting the job of spokesperson. Moreover, although we credit that
Cristofaro had no ill intent, “the standard for determining when an employer’s conduct
reasonably tends to interfere with the free exercise of protected rights is objective and
does not turn on an employer’s motive…” Hartford Board of Education, 5203 p. 6
(2021) and cases cited therein. Accordingly, we find that Cristofaro’s statements
regarding the abundance of 9th grade teachers and teacher transfers violated the Act.
Direct dealing
Turning to the Union’s remaining claim, an employer engages in direct dealing
when it ignores the union’s status as exclusive representative and its statutory obligation
“to deal with the employees through the union rather than dealing with the union through
the employees.” West Hartford Education Association v. DeCourcy, 162 Conn. 566, 593
(1972). “The element of negotiation is critical. Another crucial factor in these cases is
whether or not the communication is designed to undermine and denigrate the union.” Id.
(Citation omitted). In this case, the record does not reflect negotiations nor do we find
that Hoffman’s email evinces an attempt to elicit such negotiations or denigrates the
Union in any way. Accordingly, this claim is dismissed.
Remedy
Although the fact that the School Board never disciplined Barrows is not a
defense to a charge of interference with the free exercise of protected rights, in this case it
is relevant to remedy in that it eliminates the need for make whole relief. Nor do we
believe that this case warrants an award of attorneys’ fees as the respondent’s proffered
defense presents a debatable issue and is not wholly frivolous. See City of Shelton,
Decision No. 5296 (2023) and cases cited therein. Accordingly, we find that a cease and
desist order will best effectuate the policies of the Act.
ORDER
By virtue of and pursuant to the power vested in the Connecticut State Board of
Labor Relations by the School Board-Teacher Negotiation Act, it is hereby
ORDERED that the Hartford Board of Education shall:
I. Cease and desist from interfering, restraining or coercing certified professional
employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in the Act.
II. Take the following affirmative steps which the Board finds will effectuate the
purposes of the Act:
9

A. Post immediately and leave posted for a period of sixty (60) consecutive days
from the date of the posting, in a conspicuous place where the members of the
bargaining unit customarily assemble, a copy of this Decision, Order and
Partial Dismissal of Complaint in its entirety.
B. Notify the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations at its offices at 38
Wolcott Hill Road, Wethersfield, Connecticut, within thirty (30) days of the
receipt of this Decision, Order and Partial Dismissal of Complaint of the steps
taken by the Hartford Board of Education to comply herewith.

DECISION, ORDER AND PARTIAL DISMISSAL OF COMPLAINT
On March 9, 2023, the Suffield Firefighters Association, Local 3565, IAFF (the Union)
filed a complaint with the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations (the Labor Board),
amended on June 5 and June 23, 2023, alleging that the Town of Suffield (the Town) violated the
Municipal Employee Relations Act (MERA or the Act) by unilaterally changing the working
conditions of the position of fire lieutenant and retaliating against a member for engaging in
protected concerted activity.
After the requisite preliminary steps had been taken, the matter came before the Labor
Board for a formal hearing on June 12, 2023. Both parties appeared, were represented by
counsel, and were allowed to present evidence, examine and cross-examine witnesses, and make
argument. Both parties filed briefs, which were received on September 8, 2023. Based on the
entire record before us, we make the following findings of fact and conclusions of law and issue
the following Decision, Order and Partial Dismissal of Complaint.
1

FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The Town is a municipal employer under the Act.
2. The Union is an employee organization under the Act and at all relevant times has been
the bargaining representative for a unit of all full-time paid (“career”) firefighters employed by
the Town, which includes the positions of firefighter, senior firefighter, lieutenant and captain
and excludes the fire chief. At all times relevant hereto, the bargaining unit has consisted of 6
career firefighters. (Ex. C3).
3. At all times relevant hereto, the Town and the Union have been parties to a collective
bargaining agreement, effective July 1, 2021 through June 30, 2024, which states, in relevant
part:
ARTICLE VII
HOURS OF WORK
***
Section 7.7 Hours worked in excess of forty (40) hours per week shall be
compensated at one and one-half the employee’s regular hourly rate of pay…
***
ARTICLE XVII
WAGES
***
Section 17.1 The wage rates for all employees covered by this collective
bargaining agreement shall be set forth in Appendix A…[1]
***
(Ex. C3) (Footnote added).
4. At all times relevant hereto, the Suffield Fire Department (SFD) consisted of 4 fire
houses staffed by 6 career firefighters and 30 volunteers. The SFD is overseen by elected
members of the Town’s Fire Commission. Prior to July 2020, the SFD was managed by fire chief
Charles Flynn and a captain.
1 Appendix A contains a 6-step pay scale for the classifications of firefighter, senior firefighter, lieutenant, and
captain in each contract year. (Ex. C3).
2

5. At all times relevant hereto, the job description for lieutenant (career) in the SFD has
stated, in relevant part:
PRINCIPAL ACCOUNTABILITIES
Including but not limited to the following:
NON-EMERGENCY
• Develop monthly schedule for performance of routine inspections of
assigned apparatus equipment in accordance with Department guidelines.
• Review inspection reports to ensure inspections are completed; forms are
properly filled out, all deficiencies corrected and forms appropriately filed.
• Delivers all required paperwork to appropriate officer as required by
departments policies [sic] and standard operating guidelines.
• Coordinate, oversee and document annual pump test in accordance with
Department guidelines.
• Attends training and education programs commensurate with their duties
and responsibilities to enhance their professional development and
department operations.
• Personally inspect assigned apparatus and equipment on routine schedule.
Check general condition of vehicle and equipment for compliance with
test and maintenance requirements and overall condition and readiness for
response. Arrange corrective action as needed.
• Schedule work details as needed.
• Attend Training Committee meetings, inform Committee of training needs
and assist with instruction of Company and Department personnel.
• Conduct minimum of six (6) Company-level training classes per year.
• Attend scheduled Officer’s meetings.
• Schedule, coordinate, oversee and document yearly inspections of
personal protective equipment, radios and other Department equipment
issued to Company personnel in accordance with Department guidelines.
3

• Schedule, coordinate, oversee and document inventory of all equipment on
assigned apparatus.
• Schedule, coordinate and oversee training of personnel for
Driver/Operator of assigned apparatus in accordance to department
guidelines.

(Ex. C4).
6. At all times relevant hereto, the job description for fire chief in the SFD has stated, in
relevant part:
GENERAL DESCRIPTION
The Fire Chief ... is responsible for all managerial functions and command of the
Fire Department and Fire Marshal’s Office, including, but not limited to, financial
management, personnel management, fire prevention, planning, maintenance,
training, community relations, communications, and safety and health. The Chief
assigns various administrative and command functions to other officers or
personnel in order to maintain efficiency and ensure execution of the duties.
***
PRINCIPAL ACCOUNTABILITIES
***
