***
• Administers approved stipend and tax rebate programs.
***
• Reports to the Board of Fire Commissioners on a monthly basis on Fire
Department activities.
***
• Manages day to day operations of Department.
***
5

• Responds to emergencies, as needed, assume command, when appropriate.
***
• Oversees operational readiness of department facilities, equipment and
apparatus.
***
QUALIFICATIONS
***
• Minimum of Ten (10) years experience in a fire department with similar
responsibilities in fire protection and suppression as provided by the
[SFD], minimum of five years experience as a Firefighter or higher and
minimum five (5) years experience as a Line Officer or higher.
• Certified to NFPA 1021 Standard for Fire Officer Professional
Qualifications … to the Fire Officer III level or equivalent...
***
(Ex. C6).
7. At all relevant times since January 2018, Brian Gauthier has been the sole career
lieutenant in the SFD and a member of the bargaining unit.
8. In late June 2021, Gauthier covered for chief Flynn for one week while Flynn was on
vacation. Gauthier was paid for those hours at the higher captain’s rate.
9. In July 2020, the captain retired and the Town left the rank of captain vacant.
10. On November 17, 2021, Colin Moll was elected first selectman. Almost immediately
thereafter, in preparation for the 2022-2023 budget-making process, Moll had discussions with
the Fire Commission and the chief about the organization of the SFD, including whether to
defund the rank of captain or the rank of lieutenant. Moll contended that the SFD did not need
three officers to lead five career firefighters.
11. On or about December 16, 2022, fire chief Charles Flynn resigned. Moll met with
Gauthier to discuss assuming command of the department. Gauthier initially questioned his own
qualifications, but later agreed. In an email to the entire SFD of even date, Moll stated, in
relevant part:
The Fire Commission and myself are putting Brian Gauthier in charge of the entire
Suffield Fire Department in the interim as we move forward with plans for the
6

Department in the future. We will work closely with Brian and support him as
needed. The chain of command continues as is with the only exception of Brian
Gauthier running the department.
***
(Ex. C8).
12. Gauthier continued to perform his regular lieutenant’s duties and receive his regular
compensation. In addition, Gauthier also approved time and payroll; approved expenditures and
balanced accounts; issued low level discipline on one occasion; registered Town vehicles;
scheduled physicals; prepared tax abatements and stipends for volunteers; signed-up members
for classes; signed permits, and delivered the chief’s report at Fire Commission meetings.2
13. In late December 2022 or early January 2023, Moll met with Gauthier and Union
president Zachary Louis to discuss the chief’s duties and related issues.3
14. In January 2023, the Union filed a grievance contesting Gauthier’s compensation.
2 Gauthier testified that he devoted 1-2 hours every 2 weeks to payroll; 4 hours per week to paying bills; and 4 hours
per month to preparing the chief’s report.
3 Gauthier and Louis testified that they requested that Gauthier be paid at the contract rate for captain while he
performed the chief’s duties. Moll testified that he does not recall discussing compensation.
Q … At any point in time did you convey to the lieutenant that he would be paid at a higher
rate for the period of time he served in [the chief’s] role?
A No. It's a chain of command.
Q And what do you mean by that?
A It's a chain of command. It's a paramilitary department where if the chief is gone, the next
person takes that responsibility of the role, which is the captain. If the captain isn't there, then the
next person takes the responsibility of those roles. And that happens to fall on the lieutenant because
we didn’t have a chief or captain at the time.
***
Q And when the lieutenant takes over as captain, what rate of pay does that person receive?
A Lieutenant will receive a lieutenant pay.
Q Even while they're serving as captain?
A Under the chain of command process, yes.
C. Moll testimony, Transcript (Tr.) pp. 78, 99.
7

15. On February 23, 2023, the Town Board of Fire Commissioners (the Fire Commission)
held a meeting. The minutes from that meeting state, in relevant part:
J. Caron stated that he would rather have a Chief and Captain, not a Chief and
Lieutenant. Caron motioned to de-fund the Lieutenant position and re-fund the
Captain position.[4]
However, the Fire Commission subsequently voted to approve the SFD’s budget without change.
The minutes state, in relevant part:
J. Caron moved to accept the budget “as is”. P. Yetsky seconded the motion. All in
favor. 5-0.
***
(Ex. C6)(Footnote added).
16. On March 9, 2023, the Union filed the instant complaint.
17. On March 15, 2023, the Town’s Board of Selectmen held a meeting. The minutes from
that meeting state, in relevant part:
First selectman Moll explained that the Fire Commission had approved the decision
to un-fund the Lieutenant position at their February meeting this year as they
thought it would be better to have two officers to potentially six (6) firefighters as
opposed to three (3) officers to five (5) firefighters.[5]
***
Selectman Mahoney motioned to un-fund the Lieutenant position into the FY2023-
2024 [SFD] budget and create an additional Firefighter position. Vote: 4-0 in favor.
Motion passed unanimously.
***
(Ex. C7)(Emphasis omitted; footnote added).
18. On March 23, 2023, the Town hired a new fire chief and Gauthier returned to performing
his regular duties. Performing the duties of the chief never prevented Gauthier from performing
his regular duties as lieutenant. However, Gauthier worked an average of approximately 3.7
4 Under the collective bargaining agreement, captains are paid more than lieutenants. (Ex. C3).
5 Moll represented that he agreed with the Fire Commission's decision and that the budget had been approved with a
slightly different structure and, therefore, he felt this issue should be brought to the Board of Selectman. (Ex. C7).
8

more hours of overtime per biweekly pay period than he did in the 25 pay periods in calendar
year 2022. (Ex. R2).
19. On June 29, 2023, the Town informed Gauthier that the Board of Selectmen eliminated
the rank of lieutenant and that it was demoting him to the rank of firefighter. (Ex. C9).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. An employer’s unilateral change in an existing condition of employment involving a
mandatory subject of bargaining will constitute a refusal to bargain in good faith and a prohibited
practice unless the employer proves an adequate defense.
2. A condition of employment may be established by past practice where the complainant
shows that the employment practice was clearly enunciated and consistent, that it endured over a
reasonable length of time, and that it was an accepted practice by both parties. The complaining
party has the initial burden of showing that there existed a fixed practice and a clear departure
from that practice.
3. Employer discrimination and retaliation against employees for engaging in protected,
concerted activity is a violation of the Act.
4. The Town did not violate the Act by assigning duties of the fire chief to lieutenant
Gauthier between December 16, 2022 and March 23, 2023.
5. The Town retaliated against Gauthier in violation of the Act.
DISCUSSION
The Union contends that the Town made a unilateral change to Gauthier’s job duties and
workload in violation of Section 7-470(a)(1) and (4)6 of the Act by assigning Gauthier to the
duties of the fire chief and unfunding his position in retaliation for filing this complaint. The
Union also argues that Gauthier received increased compensation in the past when he filled in for
the chief. The Union seeks an order finding that the Town violated Act, reinstating Gauthier to
the rank of lieutenant and making him whole for any losses, and granting such other relief as will
effectuate the purposes of the Act.
6 Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-470 states, in relevant part:
(a) Municipal employers or their representatives or agents are prohibited from: (1) Interfering,
restraining or coercing employees in the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7-468… (4)
refusing to bargain collectively in good faith with an employee organization which has been
designated in accordance with the provisions of said sections as the exclusive representative of
employees in an appropriate unit…
***
9

The Town responds that the lieutenant’s job responsibilities include assuming command
of the SFD in the absence of a superior officer, any impact on Gauthier’s workload was
diminimis as demonstrated by only a slight increase in average overtime hours, and that the
Union failed to establish a past practice of paying lieutenants at a higher rate for performing the
duties of the chief. Regarding retaliation, the Town argues that discussions about the
organizational structure of the Fire Department, including whether to defund the lieutenant's
position predated the protected activity alleged in this case. Based on the entire record before us,
we find that the Town did not make an unlawful unilateral change. However, we find that the
Town retaliated against Gauthier for engaging in protected concerted activity.
It is by now well established that an employer violates the Act when, absent a
defense, it unilaterally changes an existing condition of employment that is a
mandatory subject of bargaining. Shepaug Valley Regional School District,
Decision No. 4765 (2014); State of Connecticut, Judicial Branch, Decision No.
4532 (2011); Norwalk Third Taxing District, Decision No. 3695 (1999);
Bloomfield Board of Education, Decision No. 3150 (1993); City of Stamford,
Decision No. 2680 (1988). It is the Union’s initial burden to make a prima facie
case establishing that a change in an existing condition of employment has in fact
occurred, for if no change is proven, no further inquiry is warranted. State of
Connecticut, Decision No. 4573 (2012); Town of Hamden, Decision No. 2364
(1985). A condition of employment may be established by past practice where the
complainant shows that the employment practice was “clearly enunciated and
consistent, [that it] endured[d] over a reasonable length of time, and [that it was] an
accepted practice by both parties.”(Emphasis in original, internal quotation marks
omitted). Board of Education of Region 16 v. State Board of Labor Relations, 299
Conn. 63, 73 (quoting Honulik v. Greenwich, 293 Conn. 698, 719 n. 33 (2009)).
Once the Union has made its prima facie case, the burden shifts to the employer to
establish an adequate defense. Norwalk Third Taxing District, Decision No. 3695
(1999).
City of Danbury, Decision No. 4975 p. 6 (2017).
In this case, the Union argues that the Town made significant changes to the established
job duties and workload of the fire lieutenant. However, we are not persuaded. “We have long
believed that “the power to reassign employees to other duties which are concededly within the
job description of those employees is fundamental to the operation of any public agency and
therefore involves the exercise of managerial discretion.” Town of Middlebury, Decision No.
5003 p. 9 (2018). Although Moll’s email characterized Gauthier as stepping into the role of
chief, the record reveals that Gauthier took on scheduling, payroll, and billpaying functions
which were a logical extension of the administrative duties in the fire lieutenant’s job
description.7 (Ex. C4).
7 We also find it significant that the SFD operated without a captain from July 2020 to December 2022. In our view,
the lack of an intermediate rank for more than two years diminishes the claim of a clear demarcation between the
administrative duties of fire chief and lieutenant.
10

Similarly, we find that the Union has failed to establish a prima facie case with regard to
the alleged change to Gauthier’s workload. “[A]ction by an employer which substantially
increases workload over historic levels may constitute an illegal refusal to bargain. Town of
Hamden, Decision No. 2364 (1985) (Internal citations omitted). However, “the union must
present evidence both that the employees’ workload after the change was substantially greater
than before it and that the preceding workload had ‘endure[d] over a reasonable length of time,
and [that it was] an accepted practice by both parties.’” Board of Education of Region 16 v.
State Board of Labor Relations, 299 Conn. 63, 79 (2010) (quoting Honulik v. Greenwich, 293
Conn. 698, 719 n. 33). In this case, Gauthier testified that he was able to perform all of his usual
duties during the entire period from December 16, 2022 through March 23, 2023 and while
Gauthier experienced a modest increase in his average weekly overtime, payroll records from the
preceding 25 consecutive pay periods show that fluctuations in Gauthier’s overtime hours were
not uncommon. Based on this record, we find that the Union failed to establish a substantial
increase in workload. Town of Hamden, supra; Board of Education of Region 16, supra, 299
Conn. at 79. Lastly, while the Town paid Gauthier one week of captain’s pay in 2021, it is the
only evidence in the record of paying additional compensation to a lieutenant for temporarily
performing the duties of the chief. As such, the Town’s failure to do the same here does not
satisfy the Union’s burden since “a single instance does not a past practice make.”8 City of
Bridgeport, Decision No. 5007 p. 8 (2018); see also Town of Ridgefield, Decision No. 5163
(2021).
Although the Union failed to establish a prima facie case of unilateral change, the Town’s
subsequent elimination of Gauthier’s rank is more troubling.
A complainant alleging that employees were discriminated against in their
employment because of [protected, concerted] activity has the initial burden of
showing that the discriminatory action was taken because of these protected
activities, or at least that the protected activities were a substantial factor in bringing
about these adverse actions. Town of Greenwich, Decision No. 2257 (1983), aff’d
O’Brien v. State Board of Labor Relations, 8 Conn. App. 57 (1986); Connecticut
Yankee Catering Co., Inc. Decision No. 1601 (1977). We determine whether the
complainant has met this burden to establish a prima facie case of discrimination
using an analytical framework such as is found in Wright Line, 251 NLRB 1083,
enfd 622 F.2d 899 (1st Cir. 1981), cert denied 455 U.S. 989 (1982) … Once a prima
facie case is established, we then address whether the employer has established an
affirmative defense which may include proof that the employer would have pursued
its course of conduct regardless of any anti-union motivation. City of Hartford,
Decision No. 3785 (2000); New Fairfield Board of Education, Decision No. 3327
(1995).
8 We take no position here on whether or to what extent the Union may raise the issue of additional compensation at
the bargaining table. See Waterbury Teachers Association, Decision No. 2337 (1984) (stating that the salary a
teacher will receive while temporarily performing duties of a school administrator is a mandatory subject of
bargaining).
11

***
City of Shelton, Decision No. 5298 p. 7 (2023).
A prima facie case includes proof that: (1) the employee engaged in protected, concerted
activities; (2) the employer had knowledge of those activities; and (3) the employer harbored
anti-union animus. New Britain Board of Education, Decision No. 4290 (2008). Filing a
grievance or a prohibited practice complaint is within the scope of protected, concerted activity.
Town of Trumbell, Decision No. 3056 (1992); City of New Britain (Kosinski), Decision No.
1131 (1973), rev'd on other grounds, Henry Kosinski v. Connecticut State Board of Labor
Relations, Superior Court, judicial district of Hartford, Docket No. 181823 (Jan. 1974). There is
no real dispute that the Town had notice of the protected activity in this case. Therefore, the
critical question is whether the Town harbored anti-union animus.
Animus or improper intent is ordinarily established by inference.
“In this day and age, discrimination is almost invariably conducted surreptitiously;
employers who engage in this form of misconduct do not do so overtly.” Town of
Watertown, Decision No. 3719 (1999). Factors such as statements by the employer
and the relation in time between the protected activity and the employer’s action
are important in determining whether discrimination has occurred. Town of
Wallingford, Decision No. 3662 (1999). Because direct evidence of discriminatory
motive so frequently is unavailable, the Union is entitled to the benefit of
reasonable inferences under the circumstances. Hartford Board of Education,
Decision 4544 (2011); Town of Hamden (Police), Decision No. 2394 (1985).
***
Town of Cheshire, Decision No. 4809 p. 9 (2015).
In our view, the Town’s reliance on discussions about changing the SFD command
structure occurring prior to the Fire Commissioner’s meeting on February 23, 2023 is misplaced
since that body voted to accept the department budget “as is” despite Caron’s comments about
defunding the lieutenant’s position. What we find more significant is that, notwithstanding the
Fire Commission’s vote, Moll submitted a proposal to defund Gauthier’s position to the Board of
Selectman 6 days after the Union filed this prohibited practice complaint. We find that sequence
of events, and their proximity in time, support a reasonable inference of retaliation. Nor do we
believe that the Town would have defunded the position of lieutenant regardless of anti-union
motivation. The record indicates that the Board of Selectmen’s decision was based on Moll’s
representation that the Fire Commissioners approved the decision to un-fund the Lieutenant
position at their February 2023 meeting. However, the minutes from that meeting do not
corroborate Moll’s statement. Although Moll later testified that the Fire Commission made the
decision 2-3 weeks after the February meeting, the record is devoid of any meeting minutes or
other documents to corroborate that testimony. Furthermore, when questioned by this Board,
12

Moll’s answers were unpersuasive.9 Finally, we find that Moll’s testimony that a subordinate
officer does not receive extra pay for filling a vacancy in the chain of command further supports
a finding that his actions were motivated by the object of the prohibited practice complaint (i.e.,
additional compensation).
Since we conclude that the Union has established an unrebutted prima facie case of
unlawful retaliation for engaging in protected activity, we turn to the issue of remedy. We find
that make whole relief and restoration of the status quo ante would best effectuate the policies
underlying the Act and so we order the Town to reinstate Gauthier to his former position and
make him whole for lost wages resulting from his demotion to firefighter.
ORDER
By virtue of and pursuant to the power vested in the Connecticut State Board of Labor
Relations by the Municipal Employee Relations Act, it is hereby
ORDERED that the Town of Suffield shall:
I. Cease and desist from retaliating against Brian Gauthier for engaging in protected
concerted activity
II. Take the following affirmative steps which the Board finds will effectuate the purposes
of the Act:
A. Within thirty (30) days of the date of this Decision, Order and Partial Dismissal of
Complaint, restore Brian Gauthier to his former rank of lieutenant and make him
whole for all losses incurred because of the Town’s violation, including but not
limited to back pay with interest, pay increments, seniority, and all other
employment benefits which he would have received but for the Town’s illegal
acts.
9 Alternate Member Carter asked, in relevant part:
MS. CARTER: Well, I may have missed it, but in reading through the fire commission …
minutes…, … I see Jay Caron speaking that he'd rather have a chief than a captain... And he does a
motion to defund the lieutenant position and refund the captain. But I don't see that they took a vote
on it. They took a vote on accepting the budget as is. Was this defunding in the budget or did they
just forget to vote on this particular element? …
MR. MOLL: I don't recall…
MS. CARTER: Okay. Because the board of selectman said they were voting because the
fire commission voted. And I don't see the fire commission voting...
***
C. Moll testimony, Tr. pp. 99-100.
13

B. Post immediately and leave posted for a period of sixty (60) consecutive days
from the date of the posting, in a conspicuous place where the members of the
bargaining unit customarily assemble, a copy of this Decision, Order and Partial
Dismissal of Complaint in its entirety.
C. Notify the Connecticut State Board of Labor Relations at its offices at 38 Wolcott
Hill Road, Wethersfield, Connecticut, within thirty (30) days of the receipt of this
Decision, Order and Partial Dismissal of Complaint of the steps taken by the
Town of Suffield to comply herewith.

Since the parties have agreed that the unit is appropriate, the Board’s approval of the action
herein is not to be taken as a precedent as to what unit it would find appropriate in the absence of such an
agreement.
Therefore, by virtue of and pursuant to the power vested in the Connecticut State Board of Labor
Relations by the Municipal Employee Relations Act, it is hereby,
CERTIFIED, that International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 420 has been selected as the
representative for the purposes of collective bargaining by the majority of all Water Operations and Water
Treatment Employees including Assistant Crew Chief, Distribution Operators, Meter Reader, Assistant
Chief Production Operator and Production Operators, excluding Guards. and that said International
Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 420, is the exclusive representative of all said employees for
the purposes of collective bargaining with respect to wages, hours and other conditions of employment.
